title: The varieties
hookLine: William James described mystical experience as hard to put into words, yet felt as knowledge (The Varieties of Religious Experience)

cards: "So how was it?" Someone asks after the birth, the funeral, the night on the mountain, the concert where the whole room went quiet. And the answer comes out thin: "It was... amazing. You kind of had to be there."
The speaker knows that's not it. So does the listener. Something real happened, and the words came back nearly empty.

The American psychologist and philosopher William James took that awkward moment seriously. He gathered people's own accounts of their biggest experiences and noticed the same stumble again and again.

teach.b: His book is The Varieties of Religious Experience. Varieties, plural, on purpose: James wasn't defending one church or attacking another.
He filled the pages with first-person letters and memoirs from very different people, then asked what they had in common. First, the mark he called ineffability.
The person says it defies expression; no report in words seems adequate. James compared it to music or to love: to know it, it seems you have to have been there. Second, the surprise.
Something that can't be put into words, you'd think, would feel vague. James said these states feel the opposite.

He called that their noetic quality: they seem to the person to be knowledge, insight, something learned and not just felt, often carrying a sense of authority long afterward. Hard to say, and yet known.
Third, James's honesty about himself. He admitted his own temperament kept him almost entirely out of such states.
He wrote about them from the outside, carefully, without mocking and without claiming more than he'd seen. Fourth, a neighbor who said it long before him.

teach.h: HARD TO SAY, AND YET KNOWN.
teach.b: The Tao Te Ching, the Chinese classic that tradition credits to Laozi, opens, in James Legge's translation: "The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao."
The Way itself is what the words keep missing. That doesn't make the words useless. It makes them honest when they stumble.

how: Readers of William James use his marks of mystical experience, especially ineffability and the noetic quality, to talk about religious and nonreligious experiences alike; some people keep a journal to try to put such moments into words.

games.q: you're William James. letter after letter describes a moment the writer says can't be put into words. what do you do with them?
o: dismiss them: if it can't be said, it isn't real.
take them seriously and ask what they share.
keep only the ones from your own church.
games.why: he took them seriously, set them side by side, and named their marks: hard to say, and yet felt as knowledge.

practice: Pick one big moment of your own and try to describe it silently, in three or four sentences, as if to a friend.

Notice exactly where the words start to slip, the sentence that comes out flatter than the thing itself, and stay at that edge without fixing it. If you pray, you can let the unspoken part be your prayer.
